section: Section B - History and Development of Physical Education and Sport
title: Structured: purposes of sport in ancient societies and the benefits of PE today
source:
At your school's orientation for new students, the principal has asked you, as captain of the sports club, to give a short speech on why physical education and sport matter. You want the speech to show that organised sport is not a new idea: societies have trained, competed and held contests for centuries, and the modern Olympic Games, revived in Athens in 1896, grew out of that tradition.

Your school now enters island-wide competitions in athletics, netball, football, cricket and swimming, and three of last year's leavers have gone on to national junior squads.
prompt: Answer ALL parts of this question. This is ONE of FIVE compulsory questions of the written paper: in the real examination these five 9-mark structured questions are Paper 01 Section B (1 hour 30 minutes, 45 marks). Physical Education and Sport has no written Paper 02 - Paper 02 is the practical assessment carried out by an external examiner - so this written section is the subject's only pen-and-paper paper.
planningHints: Count the points the question asks for before you write: THREE purposes and THREE benefits means six separate points, and each one must be different from the others.
'State' is a 1-mark verb: one clear sentence per point is enough, so keep part (a) short and save your time for the explanations in part (b).
'Explain' is worth 2 marks per point: write the benefit, then add what it does for the young person. A list of three benefits with no reasons can only earn half of the 6 marks.
Budget about 18 minutes for this question - the paper gives 1 hour 30 minutes for the five questions.
examinerTips: Every question on this paper is worth 9 marks and the phrasing tells you how the marks are split: 'state THREE' pays 1 mark for each point, while 'explain THREE' pays 2 marks for each point. Notice that this paper is Paper 01 Section B, not a Paper 02: Physical Education's Paper 02 is the practical assessment, so these five written questions are the ones you sit with pen and paper, and the historical content comes from area 1 of the Compulsory Core.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: State THREE purposes that physical activity and sport served in the societies of ancient Greece and other early civilisations.
parts.modelAnswer: Any three of the following. Survival - hunting and gathering, and keeping the strength needed to defend the community. Military preparedness - training soldiers for war. Health - keeping the body fit and strong. Religion - athletic contests and dances held as part of festivals in honour of the gods. Recreation and entertainment - sport as a spectacle for the community. Education - physical training formed part of the schooling of young men.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any THREE purposes correctly stated (maximum 3 marks).

Accept: survival or hunting; military preparedness or training for war; health or physical fitness; religious worship, festivals or ceremonies; recreation or entertainment; education or the training of young people; competition or the display of strength and skill.
Do not award a mark for 'to win prize money' or 'to become famous' - sport in those societies was not professional in that sense.
Total 3 marks.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Explain THREE benefits that physical education and sport can bring to young people in the Caribbean today.
parts.modelAnswer:
Physical health and fitness. Regular activity develops the heart, lungs, muscles and bones and helps to control body weight, which reduces the risk of the non-communicable diseases that are common in the Caribbean - obesity, type 2 diabetes and hypertension.

Social development. Playing on a team teaches cooperation, leadership and discipline, and players learn to accept defeat and to respect opponents and officials; it also brings students from different communities and backgrounds together.

Mental and emotional well-being. Exercise relieves stress and anxiety and improves mood and self-esteem, and students who are active usually concentrate better in class.

Also acceptable: a route to education and a career (PE teacher, coach, referee, physiotherapist, sports administrator, sport journalist), and national pride and a sense of belonging when local athletes represent the country.
markScheme: 2 marks for EACH benefit fully explained: 1 mark for naming the benefit and 1 mark for the explained effect on the young person. 3 x 2 = 6 marks.

Accept any THREE of: improved physical health and fitness (with a Caribbean-relevant effect such as reducing obesity, type 2 diabetes or hypertension); social development - teamwork, cooperation, leadership, discipline, learning to accept defeat, meeting students from other communities; emotional and mental benefits - managing stress and anxiety, improved self-esteem and mood, better concentration; education and career benefits; national pride and belonging.
1 mark only where the benefit is named but nothing is explained, or where the 'explanation' simply repeats the point.
Total 6 marks.

title: Structured: the skeleton, joints and the structures that protect a joint
source:
Tamara plays basketball for her school team. During a match she jumps to rebound, lands heavily on both feet, and then pivots on her left leg to pass the ball. In the second half she complains that her left knee feels loose when she changes direction quickly.

Her teacher explains that the force of the landing travelled up through the bones of the leg and that the structures inside the knee joint had to absorb and control it.
prompt: Answer ALL parts of this question. This is ONE of FIVE compulsory questions of the written paper: in the real examination these five 9-mark structured questions are Paper 01 Section B (1 hour 30 minutes, 45 marks). Physical Education and Sport has no written Paper 02 - Paper 02 is the practical assessment carried out by an external examiner - so this written section is the subject's only pen-and-paper paper.
planningHints: Anatomy marks are earned with correct terms. Learn the names - ball-and-socket, hinge, articular cartilage, synovial fluid, ligament, joint capsule - because 'the round joint' earns nothing.
Part (a) is a 1-mark-per-point list: give three different functions of the skeleton, not three examples of the same function (support and shape are one function, not two).

In part (c) the first mark is for naming the structure and the second is for how it protects the joint, so write the word 'so' or 'which means' and then the effect. Two structures only, both explained, earn all 4 marks.
examinerTips: Parts of this question deliberately split the marks 3 + 2 + 4, exactly as the examiners do: the short recall parts come first and the explanation carries the weight. Notice that 'name TWO' needs no description at all, while 'explain TWO' needs the structure and its protective effect. Answering on the sports context in the source - landing from a jump, pivoting - shows the examiner you are using knowledge, not just recalling it.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: State THREE functions of the skeleton that are used during a game of basketball.
parts.modelAnswer: Support - the skeleton holds the body up and gives it its shape. Protection - the skull, rib cage, sternum and pelvis protect the brain, heart, lungs and other organs. Movement - bones act as levers that the muscles pull on. Attachment - bones give the muscles and tendons a place to attach. Blood cell production - red and white blood cells are made in the marrow. Storage of minerals such as calcium and phosphorus.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any THREE functions correctly stated (maximum 3 marks).
Accept: support or shape; protection of organs; movement or levers; attachment point for muscles and tendons; blood cell production in the marrow; storage of minerals.
Do not award a mark for 'flexibility' - that is a property of the joints and muscles, not a function of the skeleton.
Total 3 marks.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Name the type of joint found at the hip and the type of joint found at the knee.
parts.modelAnswer: The hip is a ball-and-socket joint. The knee is a hinge joint.
markScheme: 1 mark for ball-and-socket (hip).
1 mark for hinge (knee).
Accept 'synovial, ball-and-socket' and 'synovial, hinge'.
Do not accept 'pivot' or 'gliding' for either joint.
Total 2 marks.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Explain how TWO structures inside a synovial joint help to protect the joint from injury during vigorous activity such as landing from a jump.
parts.modelAnswer:
Articular (hyaline) cartilage covers the ends of the bones. It is smooth and slightly elastic, so it reduces the friction between the bone ends and cushions the pressure of the landing - without it the surfaces would grind and wear away.

Synovial fluid fills the joint cavity. It lubricates the joint surfaces so that they slide over each other, and it spreads and absorbs the shock of the landing.

Also acceptable: the ligaments hold the bones together and limit unwanted movement, including the sideways movement that would tear the knee; the fibrous joint capsule encloses the joint and holds the bones in place; the meniscus is a pad of cartilage that spreads the load across the knee.
markScheme: 2 marks for EACH structure explained: 1 mark for naming the structure and 1 mark for how it protects the joint. 2 x 2 = 4 marks.

Accept any TWO of: articular or hyaline cartilage (reduces friction and cushions the bone ends); synovial fluid (lubricates the surfaces and absorbs shock); ligaments (hold the bones together and limit unwanted movement); joint capsule (encloses the joint and keeps it stable); meniscus (spreads the load in the knee).
1 mark only where the structure is named but its protective effect is not explained.
Total 4 marks.

title: Structured: interval training and applying the FITT principle to a netball squad
source: The coach of a school's under-16 netball team has four weeks before the district championships. At present the players do one continuous run around the school on Mondays and play a full match on Fridays. In the last quarter of matches several players tire badly, and after training many of them are sore for two or three days. The coach has read that interval training, planned with the FITT principle, is a better way to prepare a team.
prompt: Answer ALL parts of this question. This is ONE of FIVE compulsory questions of the written paper: in the real examination these five 9-mark structured questions are Paper 01 Section B (1 hour 30 minutes, 45 marks). Physical Education and Sport has no written Paper 02 - Paper 02 is the practical assessment carried out by an external examiner - so this written section is the subject's only pen-and-paper paper.
planningHints: Part (a) needs both halves of the idea: work at a high intensity AND a recovery period, repeated. A definition that leaves out the repetition or the intensity earns 1 mark only.
In part (b) make each advantage specific to a netball player - the stop-start nature of the game, recovering between bursts - rather than saying 'it is good exercise'.

Part (c) carries 5 marks on its own: write the four FITT factors on four separate lines and give a number or a measurable guide for each one, then add one sentence that links the programme to what the team needs.
FITT stands for Frequency, Intensity, Time and Type. Every factor must be applied to THIS team - naming the four words earns nothing.
examinerTips: The applied part of this question is part (c): it is the only place where the marks come from planning rather than from recall, and it is worth more than half the question, so do not leave it until the last two minutes. Give the examiner a plan they can see: how many sessions a week, how hard, how long each work and rest interval is, and which netball activities the intervals use. The 5 marks are split four factors plus one mark for linking the plan to the team's problem - tiring in the final quarter and staying sore for days.

parts.label: (a)
parts.modelAnswer: Interval training is a method of training in which a period of hard work (an exercise bout at a set intensity) is followed by a period of recovery or rest, and the work-and-rest pattern is repeated a set number of times. The recovery allows the player to work hard again, so the method develops speed and cardiovascular endurance at the same time.
markScheme: 2 marks for a complete definition: periods of work (effort) alternating with periods of recovery or rest, repeated in sets, with the work at a higher intensity than continuous training.
1 mark for a partial definition, for example 'short bursts of exercise with rest in between' with no reference to repetition or to the intensity of the work.
Do not award a mark for a definition of continuous training or of fartlek training.
Total 2 marks.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: State TWO advantages of interval training for a netball player.
parts.modelAnswer: It trains the stop-start pattern of a netball match: the player learns to work at high intensity and then recover, which is exactly what the game demands. It develops speed and speed endurance as well as stamina, and the intervals can be done with a ball, so fitness and netball skills are trained together. Other acceptable answers: it takes less time than continuous running, it suits players of different fitness levels, it needs only a small space, and it is less monotonous than a long run.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any TWO valid advantages (maximum 2 marks).

Accept: it copies the stop-start nature of the game and trains recovery between bursts; it develops speed or speed endurance as well as cardiovascular endurance; it can be done with the ball so skills and fitness are trained together; it takes less time than continuous running; it suits players of different fitness levels; it needs little space; it is less monotonous.
Do not accept an advantage that would apply to any exercise, for example 'it is good exercise' or 'it burns calories'.
Total 2 marks.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Explain how the coach would apply the FITT principle (Frequency, Intensity, Time, Type) when planning the four weeks of training.
parts.modelAnswer:
Frequency. The squad would train three to four times a week instead of one run and one match, because the body only adapts if the training is regular; the hard sessions would be spaced with a recovery day between them so the players are not sore for days afterwards.

Intensity. The work intervals must be hard enough to reach the training zone - the coach could use a pulse count of about 75-85 per cent of maximum heart rate, or a rating of perceived exertion of about 15-17 out of 20 - and it should be measured with a watch or a pulse check rather than guessed, then increased as the players get fitter.

Time. Each work interval would start short, for example 30 seconds of hard work with 60 seconds of recovery repeated 8-10 times, and build over the four weeks to about 60 seconds of work with 45 seconds of recovery; each session would last 30-45 minutes including the warm-up and cool-down.

Type. The training must be netball-specific, so the intervals would use netball activities - court sprints and shuttle runs, jumping and plyometric drills, two-on-two attacking and defending drills - and would also develop the components netball demands: agility, speed, power and cardiovascular endurance.

Link to the team's need. This plan attacks the team's actual problem: interval training with netball movements builds the ability to keep working hard in the final quarter, and the recovery days and cool-downs cut the soreness the players have been reporting.
markScheme: 1 mark for each of the FOUR FITT factors correctly applied to this squad, plus 1 mark for linking the plan to the team's needs or to the four weeks. Maximum 5 marks.
Frequency: a stated number of sessions a week (3-4), regular, with recovery days between hard sessions (1 mark).
Intensity: the intervals must be hard, with a measurable guide - heart rate, pulse count or RPE - or a stated progression as fitness improves (1 mark).
Time: a stated work-to-rest pattern (for example 30 seconds work to 60 seconds rest) and how it builds over the four weeks, plus a session length (1 mark).
Type: netball-specific interval work - court sprints, shuttle runs, plyometric or jumping drills, speed and agility drills - not simply a longer run (1 mark).

1 mark for explaining why the plan suits this team, for example 'they tire in the last quarter, so the sessions build repeated high-intensity effort using netball movements' or 'the recovery days and cool-down deal with the soreness'.
Total 5 marks.

title: Structured: a balanced diet, food choices and fluid replacement for a young athlete
source:
Devon is 15 and runs the 800 m for his school. He trains five evenings a week after school and plays football on Saturdays. He usually skips breakfast, buys a sweetened fizzy drink and a patty at lunchtime, and eats fried chicken with rice in the evening. In his last two races he developed cramp in the final 200 m and finished feeling 'empty'.

His coach believes that what Devon eats and drinks, rather than his training, may be the problem.
prompt: Answer ALL parts of this question. This is ONE of FIVE compulsory questions of the written paper: in the real examination these five 9-mark structured questions are Paper 01 Section B (1 hour 30 minutes, 45 marks). Physical Education and Sport has no written Paper 02 - Paper 02 is the practical assessment carried out by an external examiner - so this written section is the subject's only pen-and-paper paper.
planningHints: A definition of 'balanced diet' needs more than the words 'healthy food': name the nutrients and say that the body has to get them in the right amounts.
Part (b) is about what decides what Devon eats - cost, what the shop sells, family customs, time, friends - not about what he should eat.

In part (c) each reason is worth 2 marks: give the point (sweating loses water and salts) and then the effect on Devon (cramp, early fatigue, no pace in the last 200 m). Using Devon's own symptoms from the source is what turns a 1-mark answer into a 2-mark answer.
examinerTips: Health and Nutrition questions are usually set inside a scenario, and the scenario is there to be used: Devon's cramp, his 'empty' feeling at the end of a race and his evening training are the evidence the examiner expects you to refer to. In the definition part, be precise - 'eating the right foods in the right amounts' is worth 1 mark; naming the nutrients and the needs of the body earns the second mark.

parts.label: (a)
parts.modelAnswer: A balanced diet is a diet that contains the right kinds and the right amounts of all the nutrients the body needs - carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals and fibre, together with water - so that the body stays healthy and works properly. It also supplies enough energy for the person's age, sex and level of activity.
markScheme: 2 marks for a complete definition: the correct kinds and proportions of all the nutrients and water needed for health and for the person's energy needs.
1 mark for a partial definition, for example 'eating the right foods in the right amounts' with no reference to the nutrients or to the body's needs.
Do not award a mark for 'eating only healthy food' or 'eating three meals a day' - neither is a definition of a balanced diet.
Total 2 marks.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: State THREE factors that affect the food choices of a Caribbean adolescent athlete such as Devon.
parts.modelAnswer: Any three of: the cost of food and the family income; what is available locally and in season, and what the nearest shop sells; family customs, culture and religion; the influence of friends and of advertising; time - long journeys to school or training and the convenience of fast food; personal taste and likes and dislikes; the family's knowledge and beliefs about food and health; whether there is a fridge or somewhere to cook; Devon's own training schedule.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any THREE factors correctly stated (maximum 3 marks).

Accept: cost or family income; local availability and season; family customs, culture or religion; friends or peer influence; advertising and the media; time or convenience; taste and preferences; nutrition knowledge and beliefs; storage or cooking facilities; the training schedule.
Do not accept 'he is hungry' or 'he likes fizzy drinks' on its own - a factor must explain why the choice is made.
Total 3 marks.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Explain TWO reasons why fluid replacement is important for Devon during and after training.
parts.modelAnswer:
Training makes the body lose water and salts through sweating, so without fluid replacement Devon becomes dehydrated. A dehydrated athlete has a higher body temperature and a higher heart rate and tires sooner, which is why he loses pace - and feeling 'empty' - in the final 200 m of his races.

The loss of fluid and of electrolytes with the sweat can cause muscle cramp. Drinking water, or a sports drink containing sodium and a little carbohydrate, before, during and after training replaces what has been lost, so the muscles can keep working during the race and recover before the next session.

Also acceptable: water is needed to transport nutrients and to cool the body by sweating, and replacing fluid between sessions stops him starting the next session already dehydrated.
markScheme: 2 marks for EACH reason fully explained: 1 mark for the point and 1 mark for its effect on the athlete. 2 x 2 = 4 marks.

Accept any TWO of: sweating causes loss of water and salts, leading to dehydration and reduced performance (higher body temperature or heart rate, early fatigue, loss of pace); loss of fluid and electrolytes causes muscle cramp; water is needed to transport nutrients and to cool the body; replacing fluid speeds recovery between sessions and prevents starting the next session dehydrated.
1 mark only where the reason is named with no effect explained.
A general statement such as 'water is good for you' earns 1 mark; linking the reason to Devon, to cramp or to the 800 m earns the full 2 marks.
Total 4 marks.

section: Section B - Trends and Social Issues
title: Structured: barriers for girls, inclusion of athletes with a disability, and a doping case
source:
A national review of school sport reports that: fewer girls than boys take part in organised school competitions; athletes with a disability appear in very few national events; and a sprinter who is a household name has just been suspended after testing positive for a banned substance.

The same review notes that television coverage of regional sport has grown and that sponsors are investing more money in school competitions.
prompt: Answer ALL parts of this question. This is ONE of FIVE compulsory questions of the written paper: in the real examination these five 9-mark structured questions are Paper 01 Section B (1 hour 30 minutes, 45 marks). Physical Education and Sport has no written Paper 02 - Paper 02 is the practical assessment carried out by an external examiner - so this written section is the subject's only pen-and-paper paper.
planningHints: 'State THREE' means three clearly different points. 'No team', 'no competition' and 'nothing to join' are one idea written three ways and earn 1 mark, not 3 - give three genuinely different barriers.
In part (b) each benefit is worth 2 marks: name the benefit, then explain what it does for the student or for the school.

In part (c) you may argue either way. Say clearly whether the effect on young people is on their behaviour (copying the doping), on their attitudes (losing a hero and trust in the sport) or on the sport itself, and then explain it.
examinerTips: This question comes from area 5 of the Compulsory Core, Trends and Social Issues - the material behind it includes gender equity, the inclusion of special populations, doping and anti-doping, the role of the media and commercialisation, so an answer that uses those ideas is on solid ground. Watch the wording: 'state' is 1 mark per point and 'explain' is 2 marks per point, and in part (c) a balanced answer that mentions both the harm (imitation and loss of a role model) and the opportunity (schools using the case to teach fair play) can still earn the 2 marks.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: State THREE barriers that can prevent girls from taking part in organised sport.
parts.modelAnswer: Any three of: a lack of facilities suitable for girls, including safe changing rooms; few female coaches or role models to encourage them; family or community expectations that girls should help at home, or that sport is not for girls; the cost of kit, transport and competition fees; fear of harassment or of travelling home late after training; too few teams and competitions for girls, so there is little to join; media coverage that presents sport as mainly male; loss of confidence or embarrassment during puberty; training times that clash with household duties.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any THREE valid barriers (maximum 3 marks).

Accept: lack of facilities or of safe changing rooms; few female coaches or role models; family, cultural or religious expectations and household duties; cost of kit, transport or fees; lack of teams, competitions or playing opportunities; fear of harassment or of unsafe travel; media coverage that presents sport as male; embarrassment or loss of confidence during puberty; inconvenient training times.
Do not accept 'girls do not like sport' - the barrier is what stops them from taking part, not their supposed preference.
Total 3 marks.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Explain TWO benefits of including students with a disability in a school's sports programme.
parts.modelAnswer:
Inclusion improves the student's own health and fitness. Adapted sport keeps them active at a level that suits them, builds strength, stamina and coordination, helps control weight and so reduces the risk of the lifestyle diseases that are common in the Caribbean.

Inclusion changes attitudes across the whole school. When everyone trains and competes together, students and staff stop treating disability as something to be kept apart; the student's confidence and self-esteem grow, friendships form, and the school develops a culture in which everyone belongs and takes part - and the adapted equipment and rules often end up helping every student.
markScheme: 2 marks for EACH benefit explained: 1 mark for the benefit and 1 mark for the explanation. 2 x 2 = 4 marks.

Accept: improved physical or mental health and fitness of the student with a disability, with an effect (strength, stamina, coordination, weight control, fewer lifestyle diseases); social inclusion, friendships and increased self-esteem; changed attitudes and less stigma or discrimination in the school; the school meets its legal and ethical duty to include and to adapt activities; benefits for the whole school - adapted equipment and rules, a wider pool of talent, a better school spirit.
1 mark only where the benefit is named without an explanation.
Total 4 marks.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Explain ONE way in which the suspension of a popular athlete for using a banned substance could affect young people who admire that athlete.
parts.modelAnswer:
It can teach imitation and make doping look like the price of success. A young athlete who admires the sprinter may decide that the medal was won by the drug, that the drug is worth the risk, or that regulations can be got around - so the suspension can push some young people towards banned substances rather than away from them.

It can also cause disappointment and a loss of trust, which pushes young people away from the sport: the athlete is no longer a role model, their sponsors withdraw, and young fans learn what doping costs a performer who is caught.
markScheme: 2 marks for ONE effect fully explained: 1 mark for the effect and 1 mark for the explanation.

Accept either direction, explained: young people may copy the behaviour, or believe that doping is necessary to win, or that being caught is a risk worth taking; or they may be disappointed and lose a role model, lose trust in the sport, or see the athlete's sponsors withdraw.

Also accept an answer that sees the opportunity: schools or the media can use the case to teach anti-doping and fair play, so young people learn why doping is dangerous and banned - provided the answer explains the effect.
1 mark only where the effect is stated with no explanation.
Total 2 marks.
